name: a 401 body echoes the key
why: a provider or a gateway that refuses a key often sends it back in the error body, which a command's output then holds

name: env prints a variable a command was handed by name
why: a variable tools.builtin.env passes on reaches the command's environment, and env prints every variable

name: curl -v echoes a header whole, and the token after its scheme word
why: a header value is registered whole and as what follows Bearer, so the header line and a bare token are both cut
writes:
> GET /v1/traces HTTP/1.1
> Host: otel.example.internal
> Authorization: Bearer otel-token-0123456789abcdef
> 
* token otel-token-0123456789abcdef sent
kept:
> GET /v1/traces HTTP/1.1
> Host: otel.example.internal
> Authorization: [secret withheld]
> 
* token [secret withheld] sent

name: read_file with offset and limit returns one line of a PEM
why: each line of a multi-line value is registered, so a part of a key read on its own is cut; the body line is used because the BEGIN and END lines are parts too and would be cut wherever any PEM prints them

name: a JSON dump holds the PEM with its newlines escaped
why: the \n-escaped form of a multi-line value is registered, which is how a JSON or .env dump prints it on one line

name: a base64 copy of the key is not cut
why: an encoded or altered copy is the accepted cost: nothing is decoded or guessed, so the copy is kept as written

name: a credential held as one JSON blob is cut whole
why: a variable may hold a whole service-account document, which is cut as the one value it is

name: a k=v,k=v composite is cut whole
why: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS is one value of this shape; its whole is cut here, and the round that reads the variable registers each decoded value beside it
